metadata.narrative: Compare the effectiveness and potential long-term consequences of Universal Basic Income (UBI) programs in developed countries with pilot programs in Finland, Canada, and the U.S., utilizing data from peer-reviewed economic studies and policy analysis and commentary from experts published post-2015.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Universal basic income moved from theory to live policy testing after 2015, as automation fears, inequality debates, and welfare-reform frustration pushed Finland, Canada, and American cities to trial unconditional or near-unconditional cash transfers.

Finland's national trial, launched in 2017, paid 2,000 randomly selected unemployed people €560 a month while a control group of over 173,000 stayed on standard unemployment benefits, but the treatment group still had to apply for larger conditional benefits when eligible, muting the policy's intended unconditionality.

Because of this design flaw, only about one-fifth of the treatment group's usual benefits were actually replaced, which analysts argue explains why first-year data showed almost no difference in days worked or earnings between groups.

Finland's final evaluation, released in 2020, found a small but statistically significant positive employment effect alongside major wellbeing gains, with life satisfaction rising to 7.3 out of 10 for recipients versus 6.8 for controls, comparable to an income increase of €800–2,500 per month.

Recipients also reported less depression, stress, and loneliness, and higher trust in courts and politicians, effects researchers described as mutually reinforcing "virtuous cycles" at both individual and societal levels.

Critics such as Bloomberg's Leonid Bershidsky countered that the government spent roughly 5,000 extra euros per participant in the first year for no measurable labor-market gain, a cost-benefit tradeoff that would trouble policymakers weighing a national rollout.

Canada's most direct post-2015 test, the Ontario Basic Income Pilot, offered up to $16,989 annually for singles and $24,027 for couples across three cities before it was cancelled in 2018, prematurely truncating what commentary called the only other large-scale rich-country rival to Finland's trial.

Reported outcomes were striking: 74% of participants said they exercised more, 83% reported better mental health, and 79% reported greater overall wellbeing, with majorities reporting less tobacco and alcohol use and more employment and school retention.

Economist Kevin Milligan warned that stacking a 50% benefit-reduction rate atop existing taxes and clawbacks could leave recipients keeping only about ten cents of each additional dollar earned, and separately estimated a province-wide rollout could cost $15 billion, requiring a five-point sales-tax increase.

The pilot's abrupt cancellation triggered a class-action lawsuit alleging breach of contract and a Charter rights violation, illustrating a long-term political risk of pilot-based experimentation: reversal can undermine both participant welfare and public trust.

Separately, the Canadian Centre for Economic Analysis modeled a national basic income and projected it could enlarge Canada's economy by tens of billions of dollars annually, create hundreds of thousands of jobs, and lift 2.3 million families above the poverty line, though outcomes depended on financing method.

Canada's earlier Mincome experiment in 1970s Manitoba offers a peer-reviewed long-term reference point: Evelyn Forget's quasi-experimental analysis, published in Canadian Public Policy in 2011, found an 8.5% reduction in hospitalizations, fewer mental-health physician contacts, higher grade-12 completion, and no increase in fertility or family dissolution.

Post-2015 commentators have repeatedly invoked these Mincome findings when framing the Ontario pilot, suggesting that even historical, imperfect experiments can generate durable, reproducible evidence of downstream social benefits beyond simple employment metrics.

In the United States, Stockton's SEED program, launched by Mayor Michael Tubbs in February 2019, gave 125 residents earning below the median income $500 monthly for two years, funded by private donations rather than taxes.

First-year results showed full-time employment among recipients rising from 28% to 40% and the share able to cover an emergency expense without borrowing rising from 25% to 52%, weakening the common critique that guaranteed income reduces work effort.

Tubbs described the program's mental-health benefits as "comparable to Prozac" and went on to found Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, a coalition that has since spread similar pilots to dozens of U.S. cities, illustrating durable policy diffusion from a single localized trial.

Yet Stockton's political legacy was mixed: Tubbs lost re-election in November 2020 amid arguments that homelessness concerns and perceptions he used the pilot to raise his national profile alienated voters, while economist Paul Krugman separately argued automation is not advancing quickly enough to justify basic income as a labor-displacement remedy.
Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend, an unconditional annual oil-revenue payment running since 1982, provides the longest natural experiment on basic income's employment effects in a developed economy.

Economists Damon Jones and Ioana Marinescu found the dividend produces no overall reduction in employment, though it modestly increases part-time work, a peer-reviewed finding frequently cited by proponents including Hillary Clinton, who floated an "Alaska for America" model.

A peer-reviewed World Development study by Matthew Berman found the dividend reduced poverty among rural Alaska Native communities from over 28% to about 22% between 2011 and 2015, alongside labor-force participation that remained higher than the national average, evidence against the "dependency" hypothesis.
Beyond these pilots, expert opinion remains sharply divided on UBI's macroeconomic long-term consequences, particularly inflation and wage effects.

Economists Fadhel Kaboub and Pavlina Tcherneva have argued UBI merely "throws money at a problem," risking inflation by boosting demand without expanding supply, and favor a public job guarantee that stabilizes labor costs the way buffer stocks stabilize commodity prices.

UBI researchers have rebutted this by pointing to pilot evidence from India and Africa where injecting cash into local economies induced producers to expand supply, driving staple prices down, and argued existing low-wage subsidy systems, not basic income, currently suppress wages.

Taken together, the evidence suggests pilot programs consistently improve measurable wellbeing, health, and financial-security outcomes, and do not produce the large work disincentives many economists once predicted.

Genuine uncertainty nonetheless persists about employment effects at full national scale, fiscal sustainability, inflationary risk, and political durability once short-term pilot funding or political sponsorship ends.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

A peer-reviewed World Development study by economist Matthew Berman found the dividend reduced poverty among rural Alaska Native communities from over 28% to about 22% between 2011 and 2015, alongside labor-force participation rates that remained higher than the national average for both men and women, evidence against the "dependency" hypothesis.
Beyond these pilots, expert opinion remains sharply divided on UBI's macroeconomic long-term consequences, particularly inflation and wage effects.
Economists Fadhel Kaboub and Pavlina Tcherneva have argued UBI merely "throws money at a problem," risking inflation by boosting demand without expanding real supply, and favor a public job guarantee that stabilizes labor costs the way agricultural buffer stocks stabilize commodity prices.
UBI researchers have rebutted this by pointing to pilot evidence from India and Africa where injecting cash into local economies induced producers to expand supply, driving staple prices down rather than up, and argued existing low-wage subsidy systems, not basic income, are what currently suppress wages.
Taken together, the committed evidence suggests pilot programs consistently improve measurable wellbeing, health, and financial-security outcomes and do not produce the large work disincentives many economists once predicted, but genuine uncertainty persists about employment effects at full national scale, fiscal sustainability, inflationary risk, and political durability once short-term pilot funding or political sponsorship ends.
